title: Origen reading
hookLine: a scholar and teacher of the young who read scripture on more than one level: body, soul and spirit

cards: A teenage boy in Alexandria wants to run out and die beside his father, arrested as a Christian. His mother can't talk him out of it. So, the story goes, she hides all his clothes.
That's how the church historian Eusebius begins Origen's life. The boy writes his father a letter instead, urging him to hold firm. His father is killed, and the family is left with nothing.
And the boy who couldn't leave the house becomes, while still young, the teacher of people preparing for baptism, and a reader of the Bible people still learn from and argue with.

teach.h: SCRIPTURE IS BUILT LIKE A PERSON.
teach.b: Origen's big idea: scripture is built like a person.
A human being, he says, has a body, a soul and a spirit, and so does the Bible. The body is the plain story, the words as they stand, and that alone helps simpler readers.
The soul is what the text says to how you live: your choices, your habits, your heart. The spirit is what it shows about God and Christ and the life to come.
Not every reader is ready for every level, he says, and that's fine. Then a bolder move.
Sometimes, he says, the text puts a stumbling block in the plain story on purpose, something that can't work if you take it flatly, to make you look deeper.

His example: Genesis counts a first day, a second, a third, with evening and morning, before it mentions the sun and moon. How can there be days with no sun? For Origen, the puzzle is a door, not a mistake.

teach.h: CHURCHES STILL READ IN DIFFERENT WAYS.
teach.b: Christians still differ here: some read Genesis closely as history, some as Origen did, others hold the plain story and the deeper meaning together.
And some of Origen's other ideas were later disputed, so churches still differ on how to remember him. But his habit of reading echoes.
Whenever a preacher says this story is about Israel and also about you, that's what Origen spent his life on. Ask what a verse says, then what it says to you, then what it says about God.

how: Some Christians read scripture both for its plain meaning and for what it says to their lives and about God; monastic communities and some prayer groups practice slow, layered reading of a short passage, called lectio divina.

treat the puzzle as a door to a deeper meaning.

practice: Here's a short verse from the Psalms, in the King James Bible: "Be still, and know that I am God."
Read it three ways, slowly: its body, what it simply says; its soul, where you're not still today; its spirit, what it says about God.
If you pray, let the verse be the prayer; if you don't, let it be a sentence you turn over in your hands.
